outline.chapter_title: 1. Reinforcement Learning for Large Language Models: Why a New Algorithm Is Needed
outline.description: This chapter introduces the role of reinforcement learning in advancing large language models, especially for long-horizon reasoning tasks such as mathematics and coding. It motivates the need for stable and scalable RL algorithms by explaining the limitations of existing methods and framing the core problem that GSPO aims to solve.
subtopics: How RL helps language models improve reasoning and problem-solving
The importance of stability when scaling RL to larger models and longer responses
Failure modes of current state-of-the-art RL training for LLMs
Catastrophic model collapse in large-scale RL
Why long responses, large batch sizes, and mini-batch updates create off-policy challenges
Overview of the paper’s main claim: sequence-level optimization is better aligned with sequence-level rewards
High-level summary of GSPO’s contributions: stability, efficiency, MoE robustness, and infrastructure simplification

outline.description: This chapter builds the background needed to understand the paper. It reviews the notation for autoregressive language modeling, defines rewards and policies, and explains the two main prior RL methods discussed in the paper: PPO and GRPO.
subtopics: Autoregressive language models as policies
Query-response notation and sequence likelihood
Reward functions and verifier-based scoring
The policy optimization objective in RL for LLMs
Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO): objective, clipping, and token-level importance ratios
The role of value models in PPO
Why value models are expensive and difficult to scale for LLM RL
Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO): removing the value model via group-based relative advantages
Group sampling and normalized reward advantages in GRPO
Token-level optimization in GRPO and its practical appeal

outline.chapter_title: 3. Importance Sampling and the Core Flaw in GRPO
outline.description: This chapter explains the paper’s central critique of GRPO. It develops the theory of importance sampling, then shows why applying importance ratios at the token level is ill-posed when rewards are assigned at the sequence level. The chapter connects this mismatch to high-variance gradients and model collapse.
subtopics: The purpose of importance sampling in off-policy learning
Estimating expectations under one distribution using samples from another
Why importance weights require averaging over many samples from the behavior distribution
The difference between token-level samples and sequence-level samples in language generation
Why GRPO’s token-level importance ratios do not correctly perform distribution correction
Single-sample next-token weighting as a source of noise
How variance accumulates over long sequences
Why clipping can amplify rather than solve the instability
The mismatch between reward granularity and optimization granularity
The principle that the optimization unit should match the reward unit

outline.chapter_title: 4. From Token-Level to Sequence-Level RL: The Design Logic of GSPO
outline.description: This chapter presents the conceptual leap of the paper: replacing token-level off-policy correction with sequence-level correction. It explains why sequence likelihood is the correct object for importance weighting when rewards are defined over complete responses.
subtopics: Why sequence likelihood has a clear theoretical meaning in language generation
The sequence-level importance ratio as a measure of policy deviation
Alignment between sequence-level reward and sequence-level correction
Why sequence-level clipping is more meaningful than token-level clipping
The intuition behind treating a response as the basic optimization unit
How the proposed approach addresses the root cause of GRPO instability

outline.description: This chapter presents the full GSPO algorithm in detail. It derives the objective, explains each term, and emphasizes the role of group-based advantages and sequence-level clipping. It also discusses why length normalization is necessary for stable optimization.
subtopics: Formal definition of the GSPO objective
Sampling groups of responses from the old policy
Group-based normalized reward as the advantage estimate
Sequence-level clipping with proximal updates
Defining the GSPO importance ratio from full-sequence likelihood
Geometric-mean style length normalization of sequence ratios
Why raw sequence likelihood ratios would be numerically unstable
How length normalization reduces variance
Why clipping ranges in GSPO differ in scale from clipping ranges in GRPO
Interpreting GSPO as sequence-level reward, clipping, and optimization

outline.chapter_title: 6. Gradient Analysis: Why GSPO Is More Stable
outline.description: This chapter works through the gradient derivations for GSPO and GRPO and uses them to expose the key difference between the two algorithms. The analysis shows that GSPO gives equal weight to the token log-likelihood gradients within a response, while GRPO introduces token-dependent weights that can destabilize learning.
subtopics: Gradient derivation for the unclipped GSPO objective
Expressing the GSPO gradient in terms of token log-likelihoods
How the sequence-level ratio modulates the whole response uniformly
Gradient derivation for the unclipped GRPO objective
Comparison of token weighting in GRPO and GSPO
Unequal token weighting in GRPO as an instability source
How clipping intervals interact with positive and negative advantages
Accumulation of token-level weighting errors across long responses
Why equal per-response weighting improves robustness
Practical interpretation of the theoretical gradient difference

outline.description: This chapter introduces GSPO-token, a variant designed for cases where token-specific advantages are useful, such as multi-turn RL. It explains the stop-gradient construction, shows how the objective preserves GSPO’s sequence-level weighting behavior, and clarifies when GSPO-token is equivalent to GSPO.
subtopics: Motivation for token-wise advantage customization
Scenarios such as multi-turn RL and structured reward assignment
Definition of the GSPO-token objective
The stop-gradient or detach operation and why it is used
Constructing token-level terms that are numerically equal to the sequence ratio
Gradient derivation for GSPO-token
How GSPO-token preserves sequence-level weighting in the gradient
Conditions under which GSPO-token is equivalent to GSPO
The tradeoff between flexibility and conceptual simplicity

outline.description: This chapter explains how the authors evaluate GSPO. It covers the model, training procedure, mini-batch off-policy regime, benchmark suite, and hyperparameter choices needed for a fair comparison with GRPO.

outline.chapter_title: 9. Empirical Performance: Stability, Efficiency, and Scaling Behavior
outline.description: This chapter presents the main empirical results of the paper. It shows that GSPO trains more stably than GRPO, attains better sample efficiency, and continues to improve with more compute and harder training settings.

Evidence that GSPO avoids collapse during extended training

outline.chapter_title: 10. Clipping Behavior and the Surprising Efficiency of GSPO
outline.description: This chapter analyzes one of the most interesting observations in the paper: GSPO clips far more tokens than GRPO, yet still learns more efficiently. The chapter uses this result to deepen the reader’s understanding of noise, clipping, and effective sample use in RL for LLMs.

Implications for sample efficiency and optimization design

outline.chapter_title: 11. Mixture-of-Experts Models and the Routing Replay Problem
outline.description: This chapter explains why MoE models create additional instability for token-level RL algorithms like GRPO. It introduces expert-activation volatility, describes the Routing Replay workaround, and shows how GSPO naturally avoids the problem.

outline.chapter_title: 12. Infrastructure Implications: Toward Simpler RL Systems
outline.description: This chapter connects the algorithmic design of GSPO to systems engineering. It explains how sequence-level likelihoods can reduce dependence on expensive likelihood recomputation and why that matters for real-world RL pipelines.

outline.chapter_title: 14. Broader Lessons, Limitations, and Future Directions
outline.description: This chapter synthesizes the paper’s conceptual lessons and situates GSPO in the broader landscape of RL for language models. It highlights the paper’s implications, possible limitations, and open research questions for future work.
